lessons.title: Logical relational schema
lessons.what: Tables and references at design level: keys, cardinalities and which table owns a fact — still no storage engine decisions.
lessons.why: Move from business nouns to a checkable structure: every relationship now has a home and a direction.
lessons.when: After the conceptual ER pass, before physical naming, indexing and platform choices.
read: Each box is a table; read keys first, then the reference arrows from foreign key to primary key.
Crow's-foot marks state how many children a parent may have — claims, not constraints enforced here.
inputs: The entity list from the conceptual model
pitfalls: Do not put a foreign key on both sides.
A many-to-many without a join table hides a missing entity.
lessons.limits: Logical only: datatypes, indexes and platform types are declared in the physical model, not here.
lessons.editTask: Pick one relationship and state its cardinality in words in the label, apply, and verify the marks still match your sentence.

lessons.title: Physical representation and datatype documentation
lessons.what: SQL objects with their dependencies: which view reads which table, which table feeds which report.
lessons.why: Know the blast radius of a schema change before you make it.
lessons.when: Impact analysis before renaming, splitting or dropping database objects.
read: Arrows point from a definition to the objects that consume it.
A shared lookup table with many consumers is a deliberate coupling, not an accident.
pitfalls: Do not treat a missing arrow as proof of no dependency — dynamic SQL and applications are outside the model until declared.
Do not delete a consumer from the diagram to make a change look safe.
lessons.limits: Declared dependencies only; runtime introspection of a live database is out of scope.
lessons.editTask: Add one dependency you know exists between two declared objects, apply, and check it renders and validates.

lessons.title: Document and embedded-object schema
lessons.what: A document model: nested objects, arrays and embedded structures with their containment rules.
lessons.why: Tree-shaped data needs its own contract — tables of one row type do not describe nesting.
lessons.when: Designing JSON documents, message payloads, or any hierarchical record.
read: Containment reads top-down: each level owns the fields below it.
Arrays are plural by contract, not by current length.
pitfalls: Do not flatten a tree into parallel tables just because it feels relational.
An optional node with required children is usually a modeling mistake.
lessons.limits: Structural contract only; no validation engine runs against live documents.
lessons.editTask: Mark one field optional in the source, apply, and check the marker and diagnostics.

lessons.title: Property-graph schema
lessons.what: Nodes and edges with properties: the schema of a property graph, including which labels and properties exist.
lessons.why: Graph stores still need contracts — "schemaless" without a written agreement becomes archaeology.
lessons.when: Designing or reviewing a property-graph model (nodes, edge types, properties).
read: Node labels are types; edge labels are typed relationships.
Properties attach to the node or edge that owns them.
pitfalls: Do not model every relationship as a generic "related" edge.
Do not store on an edge what belongs to the node.
lessons.limits: Declared schema only; no graph query execution.
lessons.editTask: Rename one edge type to a verb phrase, apply, and check the legend and diagnostics.

lessons.title: Key-value structure and lookup contract
lessons.what: A key-value space: key shapes, value payloads, and the lookup contract between them.
lessons.why: Make key design a reviewed decision — it decides distribution, collisions and every access pattern.
lessons.when: Designing caches, key-value stores, or any lookup-first data structure.
read: Keys are the contract; values are opaque to readers of the key space.
Lookup paths start at the key, never the value.
pitfalls: Do not design keys you cannot construct from what the reader already knows.
Do not hide a second lookup path the contract does not mention.
lessons.limits: Contract documentation; no cache behaviour is simulated.
lessons.editTask: Extend one key with a version or namespace segment, apply, and check the contract still reads correctly.

lessons.title: Wide-column and access-pattern design
lessons.what: A wide-column layout: rows keyed for the queries they must serve, column families grouped by access pattern.
lessons.why: In wide-column stores the query writes the schema — documenting which access pattern owns which family prevents expensive mistakes.
lessons.when: Designing or reviewing Cassandra/Bigtable-style tables.
read: Read from the partition key outward: what is looked up together lives together.
Column families are access patterns, not topics.
inputs: The queries the system must answer
pitfalls: Do not model wide-column tables relationally and expect the queries to work.
Do not create a family nobody reads.
lessons.limits: Design documentation; no distribution or compaction behaviour is modeled.
lessons.editTask: Rename one column family after the access pattern it serves, apply, and check the grouping still reads correctly.

lessons.title: Semantic domains and candidate bindings
lessons.what: Semantic domains: named value sets with their rules, and which fields bind to which domain.
lessons.why: Shared meaning beats shared spelling — a domain contract stops "status" meaning six different things.
lessons.when: Whenever the same concept appears in several tables, payloads or teams.
read: Domains are named rule sets; fields borrow them.
A field bound to two conflicting domains is a defect, not a convenience.
inputs: The value sets and their rules
pitfalls: Do not clone a domain instead of referencing it.
Do not bind by name when a reference exists.
lessons.limits: Declared bindings only; the registry validates references, not your data at rest.
lessons.editTask: Bind one currently free field to a declared domain, apply, and check the binding renders.

lessons.title: Catalog, database and schema organization
lessons.what: Namespace hierarchy: catalogs, databases and schemas, and where each object lives in it.
lessons.why: Ownership and environment boundaries live in namespaces; getting them on paper prevents "it worked in dev".
lessons.when: Organizing many objects across environments, teams or catalogs.
read: Nesting is ownership: an object has exactly one home.
Cross-namespace references are explicit, annotated contracts.
pitfalls: Do not let objects drift between namespaces without a migration note.
Do not hide cross-namespace dependencies in names.
lessons.limits: Organizational documentation; no deployment is performed from this view.
lessons.editTask: Rename one schema to its owning team, apply, and check the nesting still reads correctly.

lessons.title: Hybrid local/cloud deployment
lessons.what: A deployment split across on-premises and cloud environments: what runs where, and the links between them.
lessons.why: Hybrid designs fail at the seams; the seam list is the point of the diagram.
lessons.when: Planning or reviewing any system spanning local and cloud infrastructure.
read: Environment boundaries are the thick lines — everything crossing them is an explicit link.
Data gravity arrows point where state lives, not where compute happens.
inputs: The cross-boundary links and their protocols
pitfalls: Do not leave the boundary link unnamed — it is usually the riskiest part.
Do not duplicate a component in both environments without saying which is authoritative.
lessons.limits: Structural documentation; no latency, failover or cost model is implied.
lessons.editTask: Rename one cross-boundary link with its protocol and direction, apply, and check the seam still reads honestly.

lessons.title: Data-flow diagram (Yourdon/Gane–Sarson idiom)
lessons.what: Processes, data stores and external entities with the flows between them: where data moves, not who decides.
lessons.why: DFDs expose missing flows and orphan stores that a task diagram never shows.
lessons.when: Mapping information movement through a system before deciding on implementation.
read: Every arrow is data in motion, labeled with what it carries.
Stores are data at rest; a store nobody reads is a question, not a fact.
pitfalls: Do not draw control flow — arrows carry data, not instructions.
Do not let a process have inputs but no outputs.
lessons.limits: Flow documentation; no simulation of the data actually moving.
lessons.editTask: Name one currently anonymous flow with the data it carries, apply, and check it reads as data, not control.

lessons.title: Event distribution / streaming integration
lessons.what: Producers, topics and consumers of an event stream: who publishes what, who subscribes, and the contracts between them.
lessons.why: Streaming systems fail on contracts, not on brokers; the diagram is where the contract gets reviewed.
lessons.when: Designing or auditing event-driven integration.
read: Topics are the joints: everything else attaches to them.
Consumers read at their own pace — the diagram shows subscriptions, not delivery guarantees.
pitfalls: Do not draw point-to-point links around the broker — it hides the coupling the topics create.
Do not leave the schema owner off a topic.
lessons.limits: Integration documentation; no throughput, ordering or replay semantics are modeled.
lessons.editTask: Rename one topic after the event family it carries, apply, and check producers and consumers still line up.

lessons.title: Dataset lineage and derivation
lessons.what: Where each dataset comes from: sources, transformations and the datasets they produce, end to end.
lessons.why: Every number on a report should answer "from where" in one look.
lessons.when: Auditing data products, debugging a wrong number, or onboarding to a pipeline.
read: Read right-to-left from the report: each arrow is a derivation step you can inspect.
A dataset with no recorded source is an assumption, not a fact.
pitfalls: Do not skip the boring intermediate datasets — they are where errors hide.
Do not draw lineage at a granularity you cannot actually inspect.
lessons.limits: Declared lineage; no data actually flows when you read this.
lessons.editTask: Add the missing source label to one derived dataset, apply, and check the chain is unbroken.

lessons.title: Valid-time and recorded-time model
lessons.what: Bitemporal data: when a fact was true (valid time) versus when we learned it (record time), modeled explicitly.
lessons.why: Most "history" tables answer only one of those questions; the diagram keeps both honest.
lessons.when: Designing audit trails, corrections, or any as-of reporting.
read: Each fact carries two clocks; reads pick a point on each.
A correction adds a row — it never edits the past in place.
pitfalls: Do not overwrite a fact when you mean to correct it.
Do not confuse "when it happened" with "when it was entered".
lessons.limits: Model documentation; no temporal query evaluation.
lessons.editTask: Rename one timestamp field to say which clock it is (valid or recorded), apply, and check the model reads correctly.

lessons.title: Dimensional warehouse / star schema
lessons.what: A star schema: one fact table surrounded by dimensions, with grain declared.
lessons.why: The star makes analytical queries legible — and the grain declaration prevents the classic double-count.
lessons.when: Designing marts, cubes or any reporting model.
read: The fact table is events or measurements; dimensions answer who/what/where/when.
Every fact row means exactly one thing — that is the grain.
pitfalls: Do not mix grains in one fact table.
Do not let a dimension quietly become a second fact table.
lessons.limits: Model documentation; no aggregation is computed by this view.
lessons.editTask: State the grain of the fact table in its label, apply, and check every dimension still attaches at that grain.

lessons.title: Embedding, vector and model lineage

lessons.why: A model you cannot trace to its training data is a liability, not an asset.
lessons.when: Governing ML artifacts, features and their inputs.
read: Same rules as data lineage, plus version and owner on every artifact.
A feature with no recorded source is an assumption with a GPU bill.
pitfalls: Do not let "the pipeline" be a single anonymous box.
Do not version the model without versioning its inputs.
lessons.limits: Declared lineage; no evaluation of the models themselves (inference is out of scope by decision).
lessons.editTask: Add the version stamp to one artifact label, apply, and check the chain still reads end to end.

lessons.why: Every dataset that matters needs a name attached to it — the diagram is the accountability list.
lessons.when: Establishing or auditing data-product governance.

A contract without a named consumer is a wish, not a contract.
pitfalls: Do not list a team as owner when a person is accountable.
Do not let a product have zero consumers named — it is probably not a product.
lessons.limits: Governance documentation; the contracts are stated, not enforced.

lessons.title: Trust and data-handling boundaries
lessons.what: Trust zones and what may cross them: classification per zone, and the explicit gates between zones.
lessons.why: Security reviews fail on unstated boundaries; the diagram forces every crossing to have a name.
lessons.when: Threat modeling, compliance reviews, or designing data flows across trust levels.
read: Zones carry classification labels; every arrow crossing a zone edge is a gate with a rule.
Inside a zone, flows are routine; between zones, they are decisions.
pitfalls: Do not mark a boundary as trusted because it is inconvenient to gate.
Do not let a "temporary" bridge become the permanent path.
lessons.limits: Boundary documentation; no security evaluation or certification is implied.
lessons.editTask: Name the rule on one currently unlabeled gate, apply, and check the crossing now reads as a decision.

lessons.title: Backup, restore and continuity design

lessons.why: Backups nobody has restored are a hope; the restore path is the design.
lessons.when: Continuity planning and disaster-recovery reviews.
read: Read backwards from each failure mode to the copy that answers it.
RPO/RTO notes attach to the restore path, not the backup schedule.
pitfalls: Do not document a backup without its restore test.
Do not let one site hold both primary and only copy.
lessons.limits: Design documentation; no actual recovery is executed or timed here.
lessons.editTask: Add the last-tested date to one restore path label, apply, and check the continuity read again.

Do not start the move before every row has a fate.
lessons.limits: Mapping documentation; the migration itself is not executed from this view.

lessons.why: One model, many readers — the links keep every audience on the same facts.
lessons.when: Any documentation set where executives and implementers read the same system.

Detail views are selections of the same model — they cannot drift apart.

Do not link to a view that no longer selects what the link promises.
lessons.limits: Composition documentation; navigation is a reading aid, not an application.

lessons.title: Application/container responsibilities — C4-style
lessons.what: Inside the system: the deployable containers (apps, services, stores) and their responsibilities.

read: Glyphs are icon-pack bindings on ordinary nodes — the model is unchanged.

lessons.title: UML deployment diagram
lessons.what: Nodes, devices and execution environments as 3D boxes, with artifacts deployed on them and communication paths between.
lessons.why: Deployment is where architecture meets hardware; the 3D-box idiom keeps it readable.
lessons.when: Documenting what runs on which machine or environment.
read: Boxes inside boxes are nesting: an artifact has exactly one home node.
Communication paths are structural links, not runtime traffic.
pitfalls: Do not deploy an artifact to two homes without saying which is authoritative.
Do not draw network traffic as deployment.
lessons.limits: UML deployment notation; middleware-specific models and topology discovery are out of scope.
lessons.editTask: Rename one communication path with its protocol, apply, and check the deployment still reads structurally.

lessons.title: ISO 5807 flowchart — full symbol set
lessons.what: A flowchart using the complete ISO 5807 vocabulary: the classic symbols plus manual input, preparation, display, delay, loop limits, merge/extract, card, collate, sort and parallel mode.
lessons.why: Flowcharts are the most misused notation in the world — the full symbol set says exactly what each step is.
lessons.when: Documenting procedures for a general audience.
read: Read top to bottom following the arrows; every symbol has one meaning.
Decisions have exactly the branches their labels claim.
pitfalls: Do not use a process box for a decision (or vice versa).
Do not leave a branch unlabeled.
lessons.limits: Notation coverage of the ISO 5807 symbol set; no simulation of the procedure.
lessons.editTask: Swap one step to its correct symbol type in the source, apply, and check the reading again.

lessons.title: C4 dynamic diagram (numbered messages)
lessons.what: One scenario as a numbered sequence of interactions between containers: who calls whom, in what order, for this story.
lessons.why: Static structure never shows order; a dynamic view answers "what actually happens when X".
lessons.when: Explaining a flow-through-scenario (login, checkout, failure handling).
read: Read the numbers in order — they are the story.
Each number is one interaction with a name and a direction.
pitfalls: Do not number interactions you have not traced.
Do not mix scenarios on one diagram.
lessons.limits: A recorded order, not a runtime trace; choreography conformance is out of scope.
lessons.editTask: Rename one numbered step so it reads as an action with an outcome, apply, and check the story again.

lessons.title: UML sequence diagram with combined fragments
lessons.what: A full UML sequence diagram: lifelines, messages, combined fragments (alt/opt/loop), gates and time constraints.
lessons.why: Sequence diagrams are where protocol assumptions get written down and found out.
lessons.when: Specifying or reviewing message order between components.
read: Vertical position is time; fragments bracket the conditional parts.
A guard you cannot state in words does not belong on the diagram.
pitfalls: Do not use a fragment when you mean a separate diagram.
Do not leave a reply message unanswered without saying so.
lessons.limits: Notation coverage; interactions are trace descriptions, not executable models.
lessons.editTask: Rename one fragment operator or guard to match the condition you actually mean, apply, and check the reading again.

lessons.title: Whiteboard / discovery sketch
lessons.what: A preliminary map of named concepts and their relationships. An unspecified object deliberately leaves storage technology and detailed structure undecided; it is not an undocumented SQL table.
lessons.why: Use this to expose disagreements about vocabulary before implementation choices obscure them. A shared sketch provides stable identities that can acquire fields, domains and deployment details later.
lessons.when: Start an unfamiliar project or facilitate a meeting where participants need to agree on the important things before they agree on keys and types.
read: Read the nouns in the boxes first.
Read each connecting verb as an assertion, not as an enforced foreign key.
An unselected element is out of scope for this sketch, not deleted from the model.
inputs: Questions that have not been settled
pitfalls: Do not infer a table from every rectangle.
Do not treat proximity, colour, or a crossed line as a new fact.
lessons.limits: This is an explanatory model, not an executed business system. A successful render does not establish implementation effectiveness or independent approval.
lessons.editTask: After the safe label change, review the names understood by the participants in the source. Change one additional documented assumption appropriate to this diagram, apply it and inspect every reported diagnostic.

lessons.title: Conceptual business ER diagram
lessons.what: Entities and the relationships between them at business level: names and cardinalities, no storage design.
lessons.why: Agree on the things the business tracks before any schema discussion; the diagram is the vocabulary contract.
lessons.when: Early domain workshops and any review where business stakeholders must confirm scope without reading SQL.
read: Entities are nouns; relationships are verbs with cardinality marks.
Participation marks (zero/one/many) are claims about the domain, not constraints enforced here.
inputs: How they relate, in business words
pitfalls: Do not start assigning datatypes here — that is the logical/physical stage.
A relationship without a business-readable verb is usually a missing entity.
lessons.limits: Conceptual only: no keys, types or indexes are decided by this view.
lessons.editTask: Rename one relationship verb so it reads in the business direction, apply, and check the legend and diagnostics.

lessons.why: Make cross-organisation communication explicit without pretending one party controls the other.
lessons.when: Whenever a process crosses an organisational boundary and responsibilities must stay visibly separate.
read: Each pool owns its sequence flow; message flow only connects across pools.
A message flow inside one pool is a modeling error, not a style choice.
pitfalls: Do not draw sequence flow between pools.
Do not hide a participant whose messages drive your process.
lessons.limits: Notation coverage only: no execution, simulation or choreography conformance is claimed by this render.

lessons.title: Bar chart — live records, keyed refresh
lessons.what: A data-bound bar chart over a records block: the records are the source, the chart is a projection of them.
lessons.why: Show that the chart is generated from data you can replace — the supported live-dashboard pattern is a transactional record swap, not an image swap.
lessons.when: Any metric over categories where the numbers will change but the model must not.
read: Bars read value against unit by category.
The source data block is one summary away in the Files panel.
inputs: A data block to own them
pitfalls: Do not edit the picture when the data is wrong — edit the records.
Do not reorder keyed records expecting identities to follow position.
lessons.limits: Bounded native marks and finite JavaScript arithmetic; refresh replaces records, never structure.
lessons.editTask: Use ws.replaceData on the metrics block with a second keyed payload, re-render, and confirm the model fingerprint is unchanged (data-only change).

lessons.title: IEC 61131-3 ladder diagram / relay logic
lessons.what: Three rungs between the power rails: normally-open and normally-closed contacts driving coils, one coil per rung, a parallel OR branch, and a hosted function block.
lessons.why: Ladder logic is the control-room reading of combinatorial logic: conditions left-to-right, one output per rung.
lessons.when: Industrial control documentation where electricians and engineers share one reading of the wiring.
read: Power flows conceptually left rail to right rail.
Contacts in series are AND; contacts stacked on parallel tracks are OR.
One rung drives exactly one coil — the validator enforces it.
pitfalls: A rung with two coils is an error, not a design.
Branches come from the wiring topology — you do not declare them.
lessons.limits: Common-practice ladder rendering and validation; no PLC compilation, execution or IEC XML interchange.
lessons.editTask: Change the NC contact to NO (or vice versa) in the source, apply, and reason about the changed logic before reverting.

lessons.title: Typed decision table — first match
lessons.what: A typed decision table evaluated in first-match order: the first row whose conditions all match produces the outcome.
lessons.why: Expose rule order as a deliberate design decision instead of an accident of presentation.
lessons.when: Bounded business rules where precedence must be reviewable line by line.
read: Read rows top-down: the first fully-matching row wins.
Type domains on each input gate what a row may claim.
inputs: The input fields and their domains
The rule rows in priority order
pitfalls: Row order is normative here — reordering rows changes outcomes.
A gap in the domain is a silent fall-through, not a default row.
lessons.limits: Bounded decision-table evaluation against one input record; no arbitrary rule-language execution.
lessons.editTask: Evaluate the table against one input record with evaluateDecision, then swap two rows and evaluate again — the outcome difference is the lesson.
